content: Rabies is an almost universally fatal disease, with tens of thousands of deaths occurring annually and only a few documented survivors. Globally, an estimated 59,000 people die from suspected or confirmed rabies each year, though this figure is likely underestimated. The majority of these deaths occur in impoverished, rural communities in Asia and Africa, where dog-mediated rabies is prevalent, and access to timely, affordable, and adequate post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is often limited. Most patients are initially managed in peripheral or village health centers, where resources for basic wound care and rabies prevention are severely limited or absent. Once clinical signs of rabies appear, there is no effective curative treatment, and nearly all patients succumb to the disease. Management of rabies patients should focus on palliative care to alleviate suffering and provide dignity in their final stages. Hospital care is recommended when possible to ensure adequate and respectful palliative care. Sedation with benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam, or midazolam can be administered subcutaneously, intravenously, or rectally to manage agitation and muscle spasms. Morphine may be used for analgesia, though it is often difficult to access in remote settings. Haloperidol has been suggested for restlessness, agitation, hallucinations, and aggression, but its use is controversial due to adverse effects and challenges in controlling sedation. Excessive salivation can be managed with anticholinergic agents like scopolamine. Medications should be carefully titrated to avoid excessive sedation that might necessitate intubation. Patients with rabies are often isolated due to the perceived risk of transmission through contact, though the actual risk to healthcare staff is minimal if standard precautions are followed. Personal protective equipment (PPE) should be used during procedures that may generate splashes, such as intubation or suctioning. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) should be provided to healthcare personnel deemed at risk after careful assessment. Close contacts, including sexual partners, may also require PEP due to the hypothetical risk of transmission through saliva, though human-to-human transmission has not been clearly documented. Aggressive treatment protocols, such as the Milwaukee protocol, have been attempted in rare cases but have not consistently resulted in survival without severe neurological sequelae. Survivors of rabies typically exhibit a robust early immune response, with the development of neutralizing anti-rabies virus antibodies in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). However, predicting which patients may recover remains unreliable. Aggressive management should only be considered in specialized centers with experienced teams, using ethically pre-approved protocols and after ruling out other treatable conditions. The bodies of patients who have died from rabies should be labeled as infectious but not contagious, as there is no airborne or droplet transmission. Standard precautions should be observed during handling, embalming, or autopsy. Tissues and body fluids should be disposed of as per protocols for other infectious diseases. The deceased should be allowed burial or cremation according to their religious practices. Rabies virus (RABV) is present in many tissues during the terminal stages of the disease, and caution should be exercised before transplanting organs from individuals who have died with neurological symptoms suggestive of rabies. Several cases of rabies transmission through organ and tissue transplantation have been documented, underscoring the need for stringent screening and precautions.
